title: Remote Sensing and GIS in Environmental Science
excerpt: A GSA guide to how satellites and other sensors collect Earth-observation data and how GIS turns spatial information into maps, comparisons and environmental decisions.
topic: Remote Sensing and GIS in Environmental Science
subtitle: Remote sensing collects spatial information; GIS organizes, analyzes and communicates it.
keyPoints: Remote sensing observes Earth without direct physical contact, commonly through sensors on satellites, aircraft and other platforms.
GIS integrates location-based datasets so patterns can be mapped, measured and compared.
Environmental applications include land-cover change, water resources, hazards, urban growth, vegetation, glaciers and climate monitoring.

sections.heading: Remote sensing: observing from a distance
paragraphs: Remote sensing is the collection of information about an object or area without making direct physical contact with it. In environmental science, sensors mounted on satellites, aircraft, drones or other platforms detect reflected or emitted electromagnetic energy. Different wavelengths reveal different properties of land, water, vegetation, clouds and built environments. The U.S. Geological Survey uses remotely sensed data and satellite imagery to document landscape change and improve understanding of environmental processes.

A satellite image is therefore more than a photograph. Its pixels can contain measurements in visible, infrared, thermal or other spectral bands that scientists interpret according to the sensor and application.

sections.heading: From raw imagery to information
paragraphs: Remote-sensing analysis usually involves several stages: data acquisition, geometric and radiometric correction, classification or feature extraction, comparison across time and validation. Repeated observations make change detection possible. Analysts can compare images from different dates to measure urban expansion, deforestation, shoreline change, glacier retreat, flood extent or crop condition.

Spatial resolution describes the ground area represented by a pixel, temporal resolution relates to how often a location is revisited, spectral resolution describes the wavelength bands measured, and radiometric resolution concerns sensitivity to differences in energy. These concepts help explain why no single sensor is ideal for every problem.

sections.heading: What GIS adds
paragraphs: A Geographic Information System manages and analyzes information linked to location. GIS can combine satellite images with roads, rivers, elevation, population, administrative boundaries, weather observations or field surveys. Layers can then be queried and compared. For example, a flood-risk map may combine elevation, drainage, historical inundation, settlement and infrastructure data.

The key distinction for exams is simple: remote sensing is a major source of spatial data, while GIS is an analytical environment for storing, integrating, analyzing and displaying spatial data. They are often used together but are not the same thing.

sections.heading: Environmental and policy applications
paragraphs: Environmental agencies use remote sensing and GIS for land-cover mapping, water management, disaster response, ecosystem monitoring, agriculture, climate studies and urban planning. Their value comes from broad coverage, repeat observations and the ability to integrate multiple datasets. Limitations include cloud cover for some optical sensors, resolution constraints, classification error, cost or technical capacity and the need for ground verification.
For a CSS answer, draw a simple flowchart: sensor → data → processing → GIS layers → analysis → decision. Then add applications and limitations. That structure is concise and visually strong.
